title: An easier gate than Romeo's
text: Hugo invokes Romeo entering Juliet's garden and then deflates it at once: Marius has no wall to scale, only a rusty bar that wobbles 'after the fashion of old people's teeth'. The joke keeps the idyll on the ground. This is a real garden with a broken railing, and the lovers are two very young people, not a legend.

title: Love that ruins or saves
text: 'Love has no middle course; it either ruins or it saves.' Hugo stops to say Cosette, generous and unguarded, 'would have been lost' with a careless lover. A reader who remembers Fantine and Tholomyès hears whose daughter is being spoken of. The mother met the love that ruins. Hugo goes out of his way to tell us the daughter has met the other kind.

title: Euphrasie
text: Cosette confides that her real name is Euphrasie, which Marius has never heard. The reader has known it since Fantine's chapters: Cosette was her mother's pet name for her. She decides she prefers Cosette because he does. In a book full of false and borrowed names, here is a true one shared in the dark, and then gladly set aside for the name that love uses.

title: Full light, at night
text: The chapter is called 'Full Light', yet every scene in it happens after dark, under trees, with the planets turning overhead. For Hugo the light is inward. Two people 'nearer to the archangels than to mankind' make their own daylight in a neglected garden that no one else can see into.

title: Everything except everything
text: 'They had told each other everything except everything.' Marius gives his name, his father's rank and his quarrel with his grandfather. He leaves out the Gorbeau garret, Thénardier and her father's strange flight. The reader holds all the facts the two lovers have not shared, and feels the gap between their innocence and what is known.

title: Blind to the cholera
text: The cholera that the lovers fail to notice was real. It reached Paris in late March 1832 and killed some eighteen thousand Parisians that year, including the prime minister, Casimir Perier. Hugo sets the purest love in his book against the city's worst epidemic. Happiness, he suggests, is also a kind of deafness.

title: No yesterday, no tomorrow
text: Marius 'hardly remembers the morning' by the evening, and neither lover asks where any of this is leading: they 'consider that they have already arrived'. Is this suspension the purest part of their love, or something that leaves them unready for the world? Hugo describes it with delight and gives no verdict.

title: Whitewash on her back
text: Valjean, who has outwitted Javert and climbed convent walls, notices only that Cosette has whitewash on her back. Hugo plays it as gentle comedy: the watchful father defeated by a girl who agrees to everything. The man who has spent his life on guard has stopped thinking that Marius exists.

title: The debt Marius does not see
text: Éponine's 'Good evening, Monsieur Marius' embarrasses him. He owes her his happiness and has not thought of her once. Hugo adds that Marius has not even registered that she is a Thénardier, a name his father's will told him to honour. Notice that she speaks with downcast eyes and leaves abruptly. Marius sees none of it.

title: From light to shadow
text: 'Full Light', 'The Bewilderment of Perfect Happiness', 'The Beginning of Shadow': the chapter titles of this Book follow a day from noon to dusk. Hugo marks the turn not with a disaster but with a greeting on a boulevard that Marius answers awkwardly.

title: The daughter of a wolf
text: Six armed men, her own father among them, are stopped by one starving girl sitting on a kerb. Éponine guards the house of the girl Marius loves against the family she belongs to. When Thénardier pleads that they must eat, she answers 'Burst!' Notice how fully the parent-child relation is reversed: the daughter threatens the father with the police.

title: She no longer talks slang
text: 'It is remarkable that Éponine did not talk slang.' The chapter title promises slang, and the gang speaks it. Hugo has just spent a whole Book on argot as the language of crime and misery. He makes Éponine's dropped slang a sign of what Marius has meant to her: love has changed the very words she uses.

title: The nets at Saint-Cloud
text: Éponine says she does not care whether she is found dead on this pavement tomorrow 'or in the nets at Saint-Cloud' a year hence. Downstream from Paris, nets across the Seine at Saint-Cloud caught what the river carried, including the bodies of the drowned. Her bravado is the bravado of someone who already knows where the city's poor end up.

title: Stopped by omens
text: It is not the law that saves the house in the Rue Plumet. It is a girl's threat and Brujon's superstition: two sparrows fighting that morning, a quarrelsome woman jostled that evening. Hugo gives the underworld its own rules and prophets. These men fear bad luck more than the police.

title: A prose poem in place of a scene
text: This one-paragraph chapter steps out of the street and into a forest. Ruffians become beasts of prey, and the girl at the gate becomes a spectral figure in a shroud. 'The ferocious fear the sinister; wolves recoil when they encounter a ghoul.' Hugo gives the image its own chapter so that it can sink in before the story moves on.

title: The power of having nothing
text: What stops six armed men? Hugo's answer is that Éponine has passed beyond fear: thin, coughing, indifferent to death, she belongs to 'that which emerges from the cemetery'. Poverty has worn her down to something the predators cannot grip. It is a frightening kind of strength, and Hugo does not pretend it is a healthy one.

title: Boots that let in water
text: For six weeks love has floated free of money. One sentence from Cosette brings it down: her father may take her to England. Marius's answer is an inventory of poverty: debts to Courfeyrac, a three-franc hat, boots that let in water, no money for a passport. The pride that made him refuse help now stands like a wall between him and her.

title: An address on the wall
text: Marius scratches '16 Rue de la Verrerie' into the plaster with his penknife, so that Cosette can always find him. Notice the change. For weeks the garden has been a place without writing or witnesses. Now it carries words cut into its wall, and words on a wall can be read by anyone who passes that way.

title: A word of honour
text: Marius gives his word of honour for the first time in his life, 'feeling his father beside him': if she goes, he will die. Then he speaks darkly of a 'he' who receives only in the evening, and Cosette does not understand. Hugo lets a desperate plan form offstage, with Marius himself calling it senseless.

title: What have you come here for?
text: For four years M. Gillenormand has longed for the bell to ring. When it does, joy comes out of his mouth as harshness. Hugo writes two proud men who love each other and cannot say so. Each wants the other to yield first. Notice how the old man summons and dismisses his daughter just to make Marius wait.

title: The word 'Father'
text: Marius, who fought to claim the father his grandfather erased, now calls the old man 'father' in his plea, and that single word undoes him. Gillenormand hauls him into a chair, presses a hundred louis on him and tells him to chatter about his love. Hugo shows how near reconciliation came.

title: Pamela and the lancer's gossip
text: At 'Rue Plumet' the old man recalls Théodule's tale of a 'Pamela' behind a railing, a pretty girl in the eighteenth-century sense of Richardson's heroine. Gillenormand is a man of Louis XV's century, for whom such girls are for amusement, not marriage. 'Make her your mistress' is his idea of generosity. To Marius it is a sword.

title: Father and wife
text: 'Five years ago you insulted my father; today you have insulted my wife.' Marius sets the two insults side by side: the dead father he has made his religion, and a girl he has not married. The old man runs to the window calling his name four times. Hugo leaves him with 'nothing left in his eyes'.

title: The same words, read from the other side
text: The address Marius scratched for Cosette is found by her father, who reads it as a signal to enemies or a warning to himself. The reader knows exactly who wrote it and why. Hugo uses the same twenty letters to show two worlds that never meet: a lover's tenderness and a fugitive's dread.

title: Pépin and Morey
text: Valjean fears that police hunting 'political men like Pépin or Morey' might stumble on him. Pépin, a grocer of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, and Morey, a saddler, were real republican conspirators of the period. Valjean's private danger is now tied to public events. When Paris grows restless, a hidden man is less safe.

title: A message without a face
text: 'Move away from your house.' A folded paper drops from nowhere, and a small figure in a grey blouse and velvet trousers vanishes over a parapet. Valjean's life has been shaped by documents: a yellow passport, a convict's number, borrowed names. Now the warning comes unsigned, and he cannot tell whether it is from a friend or an enemy.

title: Lamarque's funeral sounds like Chinese
text: 'Are you coming to General Lamarque's funeral?' Courfeyrac asks, and to Marius the words mean nothing. Hugo makes history arrive at the moment a young man has lost interest in everything. The revolt his friends have been planning for chapters reaches him only as distant noise from the boulevards.

title: Javert's pistols
text: Marius pockets the two loaded pistols Javert gave him for the Gorbeau ambush, 'without knowing why'. They were handed to him in the service of the police. He now carries them, unthinking, through a city at war with its government. Objects in this book keep passing from one side of the law to the other.

title: A voice through the trees
text: Hugo withholds a face at the climax of the chapter. Marius has decided to die, and the call to the barricade comes as a voice from the dark street, hoarse and half familiar. He sees only someone who looks like a young man running off. The summons that sends him into the revolt comes from someone he cannot see.

title: Why go to the barricade?
text: Marius goes to the Rue de la Chanvrerie because Cosette is gone and dying seems all that remains, not because he believes in the republic. Is that a lesser reason to take up arms, or simply a more honest one? Hugo has given his friends their convictions; he gives Marius only grief.

title: Choosing which child to sacrifice
text: Mabeuf looks over his books 'like a father choosing which child to sacrifice'. Hugo keeps an exact ledger of the decline: twenty sous for a book that cost twenty francs, a Robert Estienne sold to buy an Aldus, an Elzevir sold for the cab fare to a dinner where no one speaks to him. Poverty strips a man who has harmed no one, page by page.

title: Honesty that does not pay
text: Mabeuf handed the purse that fell into his garden to the police as lost property, since he could not believe a star had coined itself into louis. No one claimed it. Hugo gives us one more honest act that changes nothing. Virtue in this book is often its own and only reward.

title: The missing book
text: The chapter ends on a gesture: Mabeuf takes his hat, reaches for a book to put under his arm, finds none and says 'Ah! truly!' His whole life is in that habit. With the last volume sold for Mother Plutarque, he walks out towards the sound of firing, not knowing what else to do with his hands.

title: Giving the other side the floor
text: Hugo opens his history of the rising by letting the opposition speak. The 'golden mean' school says riots shut shops, depress the funds and cost twenty, forty, sixty millions a day. Hugo states their case fairly, even generously, before rejecting it. This digression teaches the reader how to judge what is about to happen in the streets.

title: Effects and causes
text: The bourgeois argument counts effects in francs. Hugo answers that if July 1830 cost a hundred and twenty millions, putting Philip V on the Spanish throne cost two milliards, and he 'would still prefer the 14th of July'. His real question is not what revolt costs but why people rise at all.

title: Two years of riots
text: Hugo writes of the riots that followed 1830 as though everyone remembers them. The July Revolution put Louis-Philippe on the throne but left most people without a vote. The early 1830s brought repeated unrest, including the silk-workers' rising at Lyons in November 1831. June 1832 is one wave in a stormy sea.

title: Insurrection and revolt
text: The chapter gives the book a key word pair. Insurrection is the whole people reclaiming its rights from a usurping fraction. Revolt is a fraction attacking the whole. 'There is no insurrection except in a forward direction.' The same cannon can be wrong one day and right another. Hugo asks us to judge every rising by its direction, not by its violence.

title: The vote as cure
text: Hugo argues that universal suffrage dissolves riots at birth by giving insurrection the ballot. In 1832 the French electorate was tiny: under the July Monarchy fewer than two hundred thousand men could vote, in a nation of over thirty million. Hugo was writing in 1862, after manhood suffrage had arrived in 1848.

title: 'We have seen this'
text: Hugo promises to tell one small, little-known episode of 5 and 6 June, changing a few names. He presents himself as an eyewitness: 'We have seen this.' The novel now claims the authority of testimony. What follows is offered as the foliage of history, the part the historians leave out.

title: General Lamarque
text: Jean Maximilien Lamarque was a real general of the Empire and a liberal deputy, hugely popular with the people. He died of cholera on 1 June 1832. His funeral on 5 June, with Lafayette speaking at the Austerlitz bridge, became the spark of the rising. Hugo follows the historical record closely here.

title: Nobody knows what happened in that minute
text: Dragoons and crowd touch, three shots ring out, and Hugo admits that 'no one knows' who began: a trumpet, a child's dagger-blow? He writes history as a crowd lives it, full of rumour, red flags, a man with a red beard pointed out. The first dead include an officer and an old deaf woman closing her window.

title: A burial and a birth
text: The title calls the funeral 'an occasion to be born again'. Lamarque, who kept the sadness of Waterloo for seventeen years, is carried through Paris with the sword of the Hundred Days. The dead general becomes a rallying point for the living. In Hugo's Paris, funerals are where revolutions begin.

title: Riot as inventory
text: Two hundred and thirty guns, sixty-four swords, eighty-three pistols; twenty-seven barricades in the Halles quarter alone. Hugo's lists turn chaos into a register. The style tells you he is writing history as well as fiction: precise, street by street, as if mapping a battlefield like Waterloo.

title: The author under fire
text: 'The author of this book' sheltered for half an hour behind a half-column in the Passage du Saumon. Hugo really was caught in the fighting of 5 June 1832, and he puts himself in the story as a witness. The novel's narrator steps briefly into the street he is describing.

title: The calm at the centre
text: A third of Paris is in the insurgents' hands. Around the Tuileries 'solitude forms', and Louis-Philippe is 'perfectly serene'. Hugo sets the boiling streets against the stillness of power. The centre of Paris has become a citadel where, he notes, no fighting has yet begun.

title: Billiards beside grapeshot
text: In ordinary riots Paris barely notices: a few streets from the firing, billiard balls click and theatres play vaudeville. In 1831 a fusillade paused to let a wedding pass; in 1839 a cocoa-seller served both sides. Hugo loves this nonchalance as a sign of the city's size and gaiety, the city of Voltaire and Napoleon.

title: This time Paris is afraid
text: Then the tone changes. Shutters close in distant quarters, eight hundred are arrested by nine o'clock, and wives and mothers ask why he has not come home. Hugo brings the rising into private houses. History is now something families wait for behind bolted doors.

title: The tocsin of Saint-Merry
text: Through these chapters one sound recurs: the alarm bell of Saint-Merry, ringing over the city. Hugo builds the night around listening, to cavalry, trumpets and firing, and above all to that 'lamentable' peal. The reader, like the households of Paris, hears the rising before seeing it.

title: Where are my two children?
text: Gavroche still wonders 'where the devil his two children are'. The reader knows they are his own brothers, though he never learned it. He spent a night with his brothers and the dawn with his father without knowing either bond. A child of eleven or so talks like a parent about the only family he chose.

title: A pistol with no trigger
text: Gavroche 'borrows' a holster-pistol from a junk shop and marches off to the wars, only to find it has no trigger. His revolution is courage and theatre without means. Hugo enjoys the joke and lets it stand for something larger: the very poor go to war with whatever they can find.

title: A gamin of letters
text: Who wrote Gavroche's songs? Perhaps Gavroche himself. Hugo makes him a folk poet who mixes the birds' repertory with the workshops'. He once spent three months with a printer and ran an errand for an Academician. The street child is given an authorship of his own, and Paris itself seems to sing through him.

title: Helping the enemy up
text: On his way to fight the government, Gavroche puts down his pistol to help a fallen National Guard lancer, and then the horse. Hugo slips the act in without comment. Gavroche wants to overturn the authorities, but he will not leave a man or a horse lying in the street.

title: Four corners of old age
text: Three portresses and a ragpicker gossip in a doorway, and Hugo notes the hierarchy even here: the ragpicker defers to the portresses, the humble rank of the refuse heap. Their chatter about cats, meat prices and the Duc de Bordeaux is the voice of the Marais, where order is a habit. To them Gavroche is just 'a bastard'.

title: A gaunt poodle
text: Gavroche, insulted as a beggar's brat, pauses to pity a starving poodle 'whose hoops all show'. The street child recognises his own kind. Like his kindness to the lancer's horse, it is a tiny gesture, and it tells us who Gavroche is more surely than his swagger does.

title: A cannonball that is a pebble
text: The barber declares he would rather die of a cannonball in the belly than slowly in bed. A crash, he turns pale, 'a cannonball!', and the old soldier picks up a pebble. Hugo sets the veteran's list of wounds from Marengo to Waterloo beside the barber's bluster, and the comedy deflates both bravado and fear.

title: What has anyone done to that gamin?
text: The hairdresser is outraged: what has anyone done to that gamin? The reader knows. This is the shop where the two little boys were turned out into the rain. Gavroche has not forgotten. His stone is a rough, street-level justice for children nobody else defended.

title: The Emperor's wounds
text: The veteran's catalogue of battles, Marengo, Austerlitz, Jena, Friedland, the Moskowa, Lutzen, Waterloo, runs through Napoleon's whole career. In 1832 such men were still everywhere in Paris, and their memories fed the crowd that buried Lamarque. The Empire is still alive in a barber's chair.

title: Not firing out of the ranks
text: Bahorel tears down the Archbishop's Lenten notice, and Gavroche is won over. Enjolras rebukes him: the Archbishop is not the enemy, and one must not 'fire out of the ranks with the soul' any more than with a gun. Notice how Enjolras wants anger aimed. His revolution has no room for spite.

title: Latin for a gamin
text: 'Hercle!' 'Para bellum!' Gavroche asks what the Latin means and approves once he understands. Hugo enjoys the meeting of the students' classroom culture and the street child's quickness. The band is a mixture of social worlds, and Gavroche picks up their language as fast as he once picked up slang.

title: An old man, unarmed
text: The chapter closes on a figure among the clubs and bayonets: an extremely old man, unarmed, hurrying so as not to be left behind. 'Keksekça?' asks Gavroche. Hugo saves the name for the last line: M. Mabeuf. The book-lover who had nothing left to sell is marching with the insurgents.

title: 'That is good'
text: Fighting, cannon, flinging the government to the earth: to each, Mabeuf answers 'That is good.' The man who once cared only for plants and books now walks with a firm step and 'the face of a man asleep'. Hugo does not give him politics. He gives him the calm of someone who has nothing left to lose.

title: An old regicide
text: The students decide the silent old man must be a former member of the Convention, a regicide. A legend forms around Mabeuf in minutes, because a revolt needs ancestors. Hugo has already shown us one real Conventionist, the dying G. at Digne. This one is only a timid churchwarden whom grief has made fearless.

title: A nonsense ballad as marching song
text: Gavroche marches ahead 'like a trumpet', singing of Charlot and Charlotte and two drunken sparrows, with refrains for Chatou, Passy, Meudon and Pantin. No Marseillaise here. Hugo leads the insurgents towards Saint-Merry to the tune of a street song, the city's own music, cheeky and light.

title: Strangers in the ranks
text: Two newcomers join the band, and Hugo names neither. One is a tall, grey-haired man of bold bearing whom none of the leaders knows. The other is a pale, slight young workman who has waited an hour at Courfeyrac's lodge asking for Marius. A crowd on the march takes in anyone. Hugo lets us see them arrive, and does not explain them.

title: Monsieur de Courfeyrac
text: 'If you call me Monsieur de Courfeyrac again, I shall call you Mother de Veuvain.' Courfeyrac's father really was M. de Courfeyrac, but the republican son has dropped the noble particle. On the way to a barricade he will not be given a title even by his portress. In this book names are always a statement of where one stands.

title: A mob does not go where it intends
text: The band means to reach Saint-Merry, overshoots it and ends up 'without quite knowing how' in the Rue Saint-Denis. Hugo keeps showing chance at work in history. The great events of a rising are placed by wrong turnings, a forgotten hat and a coffer fetched from under dirty linen.

title: A letter for a map
text: As he drew Waterloo as a capital A, Hugo now draws the Halles quarter as an N, with the Rue de la Chanvrerie as one upright. The digression is doing a practical job: it gives the reader a map of a battlefield before the battle. It also says that this tangle of streets is a real place with a three-hundred-year history.

title: A vanished quarter
text: 'All of it vanished' when the Mondétour labyrinth was opened up in 1847, and the Rue Rambuteau 'devoured' the old streets. Hugo, writing in exile in the early 1860s, describes a Paris that no longer existed. Like the convent of the Petit-Picpus, the Corinthe is preserved only in his book.

title: Carpe ho ras
text: Father Hucheloup advertises his stuffed carps, 'Carpes au gras', in his own spelling. Rain washes out two letters and leaves 'Carpe ho ras', so that 'knowing no French, he had equalled Horace'. Hugo loves accidents that turn the ordinary into Latin. The wall of a cheap wine-shop now tells its customers to seize the hour.

title: Out of pity
text: After Hucheloup's death the cooking turns execrable and the wine worse, and the friends keep coming 'out of pity', as Bossuet says. They eat on credit, pay badly and are always welcome. The Corinthe is a picture of loyalty among poor people: the students and the bearded widow keep each other going.

title: A sceptic among believers
text: While Paris boils, Grantaire breakfasts on oysters and harangues: creation is bankrupt, God patches events like a tradesman with an empty till, and the one reality is drink. He is the voice of doubt inside the ABC. Hugo gives him wit and some truth, and lets him drink himself away from the cause his friends serve.

title: Make it here!
text: Bossuet, drunk on a windowsill with his back in the rain, sees the band pass the end of the street and bellows to Courfeyrac: 'This is a good place! Make it here!' That is how the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie is placed. Hugo, who has just lectured on the causes of revolt, shows how its sites are chosen, by chance and by friendship.

title: Sent to Bossuet, not to me
text: Enjolras sends his warning to Bossuet, and Grantaire mutters that Enjolras disdains him. Among all his jokes this is the one remark said without a joke. What does Grantaire want from Enjolras, and why does it matter more to him than the funeral or the riot?

title: A city turned into a wall
text: Iron bars from the wine-shop grating, paving-stones, a lime-dealer's dray, the widow's empty casks, beams from house-fronts, a passing omnibus: in minutes the street is barred higher than a man. Hugo's catalogue shows the barricade as Paris itself, rearranged. Everyday things of the city become a fortification.

title: Non licet omnibus
text: Bossuet hands down 'the ladies', takes the omnibus by the bridle and declares in Latin that not everyone may go to Corinth: 'Non licet omnibus adire Corinthum.' The old proverb, from Horace, meant that not everyone can afford the pleasures of Corinth. Here 'omnibus', 'for everyone', is also the vehicle. Even building a barricade, these students make Latin puns.

title: 'Let me sleep here'
text: Enjolras orders the drunken Grantaire off the barricade, and the rebuke sobers him at once. He looks at Enjolras 'with indescribable gentleness' and asks to sleep there. Enjolras tells him he is incapable of believing, thinking, willing, living and dying. 'You will see,' Grantaire answers, and falls asleep. Grantaire believes in nothing except Enjolras, and Enjolras cannot see it.

title: Jesus with Rothschild's fortune
text: In his drunken dithyramb Grantaire says that if kind hearts had fat purses there would be no more poor, and imagines Jesus Christ with Rothschild's fortune. It is a joke and also the novel's question in the mouth of its scoffer. Goodness without means has been shown again and again: the bishop, Mabeuf, Marius.

title: Consolation, Arab style
text: Courfeyrac 'consoles' Mother Hucheloup by telling her that wrecking her shop avenges a fine she once paid, and Hugo caps it with the tale of an Arab father who evened a slap by slapping his daughter's other cheek. Even as the bullets are cast, Hugo keeps the comedy going. These young men laugh at the edge of danger, and the book laughs with them.

title: Spoons into bullets
text: The establishment's pewter mugs, spoons and forks go into the brazier and come out as bullets; dishcloths become lint for wounds. Notice how the tavern's ordinary life is converted, object by object, into war. Hugo lists the volunteers the same way: a breastplate of grey paper, an awl, a cartridge-box marked 'Public Order'.

title: Brothers without names
text: Pale young men and bronzed longshoremen work side by side, 'brothers who do not know each other's names'. Hugo makes the barricade a fraternity of strangers, built on a shared hope of help at three in the morning, a sure regiment and Paris rising. The word fraternity on the Republic's banner is lived here for an evening.

title: A gun for the children
text: Gavroche goes from man to man demanding a real gun; he had one in 1830, he says. Enjolras answers that when there are enough for the men they will give some to the children. 'Gamin!' 'Greenhorn!' The exchange is comic, but it raises a real question the book has carried since the Thénardier children: what place does a child have in the grown-ups' wars?

title: Correcting the newspapers
text: The papers called the barricade nearly impregnable and as high as a first floor. Hugo corrects them: six or seven feet, with steps inside, a gap at one end, an omnibus pole for a flagstaff. The novelist writes like a military historian checking the record. His precision lets the reader stand inside the redoubt and see its weak points.

title: The coffer opened
text: The square coffer Courfeyrac fetched from under his linen is opened on a table: cartridges. 'A tremor and a silence' pass through the bravest. Up to now the day has been flags, songs and furniture. Thirty cartridges to each man turn the street game into something final.

title: Waiting in the dusk
text: The alarm beating through Paris becomes a noise they no longer hear. They load without haste, Enjolras posts three sentinels, and the twilight thickens among houses 'that seem dead'. Hugo slows the prose to the rhythm of waiting. Darkness is coming in from outside the barricade, and so is something unseen.

title: Love verses with loaded carbines
text: Hugo insists on telling what they did while waiting, 'since it is history': they sat together as in their student days and recited love poems. Prouvaire's poem remembers a garret, a burnt muff, a Dante used as a table for chestnuts. These young men are not only revolutionaries. Their politics come from the same young hearts that wrote poems about love.

title: A poem inside the novel
text: Hugo stops his prose for verses, a whole poem of youth in the Latin Quarter. Its lightness, against 'the funereal calm of the deserted streets', gives it what he calls a pathetic charm. The poem looks back at a love that has passed, while the men around it wait for the attack.

title: A torch for the flag
text: The wax torch is set in a cage of paving-stones so that all its light falls on the red flag and none on the men. Street and barricade sink into gloom; the flag glows, 'its scarlet deepened to a terrible purple'. Hugo stages the barricade like a theatre at night. Only the idea is lit, and the men stay in the dark.

title: Recognition on a child's face
text: Before any word is spoken, Gavroche's face runs through 'every grimace' of disbelief, uncertainty and conviction as he circles the stranger on tiptoe. Hugo stages the unmasking first as mime. Then the questions, and the name: 'Javert.' The tall recruit from the Rue des Billettes has been the hunter all along, and the chapter makes us wait for the word.

title: The mouse who has caught the cat
text: 'It's the mouse who has caught the cat,' says Gavroche. Javert, the law in person, is bound to the post in the middle of a wine-shop by rebels. He does not cry out, and raises his head 'with the intrepid serenity of the man who has never lied'. Hugo grants him dignity even in defeat: he is wrong, perhaps, but he is honest.

title: Judges, not assassins
text: 'Then finish the business with a blow from a knife.' 'Spy, we are judges and not assassins.' Enjolras claims for the barricade the very thing Javert serves: lawful judgement. Each side calls itself the law. Javert is to be shot ten minutes before the barricade falls, and both men speak of it calmly, as a matter of procedure.

title: Prefect Gisquet
text: The card found on Javert bears the signature of 'M. Gisquet', the real Prefect of Police of Paris from 1831 to 1836. Hugo threads real names through his invented ones, as he did with Lamarque and Lafayette. A fictional inspector carries a real man's orders, which makes the fiction feel documented.

title: He killed, therefore I killed him
text: Enjolras executes Le Cabuc for murdering the old porter, then tells the barricade: 'I have judged myself also.' The reader has seen this rigour before, in Javert asking Madeleine to dismiss him for a mistaken denunciation. Hugo sets the revolutionary and the policeman as mirror images. Both are pure, both are merciless, and both apply their law to themselves.

title: Fatality and Fraternity
text: Enjolras calls necessity 'a monster of the old world named Fatality', and says the law of progress is for Fatality to vanish before Fraternity. He uses death but hates it, he says. Hugo calls him 'executioner and priest', and the speech is both a creed and a confession. His friends watch him with admiration mixed with compassion.

title: The porter who said no
text: The old porter at his window cannot even see who is aiming at him. He says 'That cannot be, gentlemen' and is shot under the chin. Hugo ends the image with a head on the sill and a little white smoke. Like the deaf old woman at the Austerlitz bridge, the first innocent dead of the barricade is someone who only wanted to keep his door shut.

title: Le Cabuc and Claquesous
text: Hugo offers, as 'a tradition of the police, strange but probably well founded', that Le Cabuc was Claquesous, the masked member of Patron-Minette who slipped away after the Gorbeau arrests. A police card was found on the body; Hugo says he held the 1832 report in 1848. A man whose life was 'all shadows' ends as a riddle, on the edge of both the underworld and the police.

title: A descent through Paris
text: Marius walks from the Rue de Rivoli, with its gaslight and ices, through shut shops with chatting merchants, then a silent crowd, then the army's bivouacs, into streets 'like a cellar'. Hugo turns the walk into a cross-section of the city, layer by layer, 'like a descent of black steps'. Each stage is darker and quieter than the one before.

title: Two white horses and a shaving dish
text: In the black streets Marius meets the two omnibus horses Bossuet unharnessed that morning, still wandering 'with the patience of brutes'. A stray shot pierces a barber's brass dish, 'still to be seen there in 1848'. Hugo uses small physical leftovers of the day, and his own memory of them, to make the night real.

title: The key to the tomb
text: To Marius the voice through the twilight sounds like destiny: he wished to die, and 'a hand in the darkness offers the key to the tomb'. Notice that he goes to the barricade as a lover in despair, armed by chance with Javert's pistols, not as a convert to his friends' politics.

title: Paris from the air, again
text: 'An owl's view of Paris' answers a famous chapter in Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris (1831), 'A Bird's-Eye View of Paris'. There he rebuilt the medieval city from the towers of the cathedral. Here, from above, the old Halles quarter is a black hole in the centre of Paris, with only Saint-Jacques and Saint-Merry rising out of it.

title: Order means night
text: 'The insurrection's invisible police keep order, that is, night': every window that showed a candle at dusk received a shot. Hugo turns his central image pair upside down. Here darkness is the rebels' protection, and the light belongs to the bayonets tightening in a ring around them.

title: The voice from below
text: Hugo sets the political battle, the schools against the middle classes, inside a deeper sound. In 'wretched old Paris beneath the splendour of happy Paris', the people roar, a voice 'from below like the lion and from on high like the thunder'. Behind the students' principles he wants us to hear the misery the whole book has described.

title: The sword that would not come
text: Marius thinks of his father's sword, sold by his grandfather, and decides it did well not to come: a sword from Marengo would not go to the Rue de la Chanvrerie. Civil war feels like desecrating Colonel Pontmercy. The dead father has become Marius's conscience. Notice that he argues with his father's ghost before he argues with himself.

title: Reason or rationalisation?
text: Marius works his way to a 'splendid rectification': there is only just and unjust war, and the monarchy is itself a foreigner. Hugo remarks on the soul's strange aptitude for cold reasoning in extremity, 'the thread of the syllogism floating unbroken in the storm'. Has Marius found a conviction, or given grief the reasons it wanted?

title: A dead man at the window
text: When Marius looks up, a spectator above the barricade seems 'singularly attentive': it is the porter killed by Le Cabuc, staring, mouth open, blood trailing down the wall. Hugo makes the dead a witness. Marius came here to look death in the face, and this is the first face he sees.
